History and Physical (H&P – Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
34-year-old male with asthma and hay fever presents with a 6-week history of generalized fatigue and diffuse musculoskeletal aching that began two weeks after returning from a hiking holiday in the United States; notes a transient annular calf rash in late February. Clinician suspects Lyme disease and orders comprehensive blood tests, including Lyme serology, CBC, renal and liver profile.

History:
• Presenting complaint: “Aching all over” with marked tiredness/run-down feeling for ≈6 weeks.  
• Onset & course: Well over Christmas/New Year; traveled to U.S. late Jan; symptoms began mid-Feb (≈2 wks post-travel) and persist without improvement.  
• Rash: Single annular lesion on posterior calf noticed by wife mid-/late-Feb; minimally itchy, resolved over ~2 weeks; photo shown during consult. Mild sore throat and possible low-grade fever occurred at same time. No current skin changes.  
• Musculoskeletal: Dull aches in shoulders, back, hips, knees; no joint swelling.  
• Neurologic: Mild nonspecific headaches; no visual changes, numbness, tingling.  
• Constitutional: Fatigue, reduced daytime concentration/energy. Appetite reduced (smaller portions) but no weight change. No night sweats reported.  
• Respiratory: No cough, shortness of breath, wheeze, or chest infection.  
• GI: No abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, or blood in stool.  
• GU: No dysuria or haematuria.  
• HEENT: No current earache or sore throat.  
• Psych: Mood and stress “pretty good.”  
• Functional impact: Attending work but less effective; exercising less than usual.  
Pertinent negatives: No additional rashes, no joint swelling, no neurologic deficits, no urinary or bowel changes.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma – stable; uses preventer inhaler. No recent exacerbations.  
• Hay fever – seasonal; self-managed with OTC antihistamine.  
No other chronic illnesses documented.

Medications:
• Preventive inhaler (name/dose/route/frequency not documented; patient uses morning and night).  
• OTC antihistamine (name/dose/frequency not documented).  
No other regular medicines reported.

Allergies: Not discussed (missing).

Social History:
• Occupation: Health-technology company employee.  
• Living situation: Lives with wife.  
• Activities: Enjoys walking/hiking; wore shorts during U.S. trip (possible tick exposure).  
• Smoking: Not documented (patient did not state; clinician asked).  
• Alcohol: Occasional consumption.  
• Recreational drugs: Not mentioned.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
No examination findings or vital signs documented during video consult.

Investigations:
• None completed yet.  
• Planned: Blood panel (CBC, renal profile, liver profile, thyroid as part of “normal things” implied), Lyme disease serology, and other infection screens as per clinician.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Fatigue, diffuse myalgia, history of annular rash; ?Lyme disease versus other causes  
  • Assessment: Timeline and rash highly suggestive of early disseminated Lyme disease; differentials include post-viral fatigue and hypothyroidism.  
  • Plan:  
    – Order blood tests: CBC, renal, liver, thyroid function, Lyme serology, and other infection screens.  
    – Arrange follow-up tele-consult ~1 week after tests to review results.  
    – If Lyme serology positive, commence appropriate antibiotic regimen (specific agent/dose per guidelines; not yet prescribed).  
    – Advice: Monitor for new symptoms (fever, joint swelling, facial weakness, palpitations) and seek care if they occur sooner.

Issue 2 – Asthma maintenance  
  • Assessment: Stable; patient uses preventer inhaler regularly but unclear about reliever use.  
  • Plan:  
    – Reinforce adherence to preventer inhaler; ensure patient has rescue inhaler available.  
    – Review inhaler technique and need for annual asthma review at next suitable appointment.

Issue 3 – Allergic rhinitis (hay fever)  
  • Assessment: Controlled with OTC antihistamine.  
  • Plan: Continue current antihistamine; consider intranasal steroid if symptoms worsen.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Lyme disease – Likelihood: High. Rash resembling erythema migrans after hiking in endemic area; onset of fatigue/myalgia follows typical course.  
2. Post-viral fatigue / chronic viral infection (e.g., EBV/CMV) – Likelihood: Moderate. Sore throat and low-grade fever at onset could indicate viral illness; persistent fatigue common.  
3. Hypothyroidism – Likelihood: Moderate. Fatigue and myalgia warrant TSH screening, though absence of classic hypothyroid features lowers probability.
